# Data tables {#sec-data-tables}

Suppose you are booking a flight out of New York and you would rather not spend the evening sitting on a runway. Which airline has the longest delays on average? Does it matter whether you fly out of Newark, JFK or LaGuardia, or whether you take a morning flight instead of an evening one? The U.S. government publishes data on every domestic flight, the airline that operated it, the airport it left from, the time it was scheduled to leave, and the time when it actually left. Using this data, it is possible to answer these questions.

When answering these questions it is important to keep information about the *same* flight together; i.e., you need each flight's carrier, the time the flight was scheduled to depart, its delay, etc. attached to each other, for all flights. This is difficult to do using the the list and arrays discussed in the last two chapters. 

A **table** makes the connection explicit. Each row corresponds to one item in the world, such as a single flight (or a movie or a particular week in the year), and each column is one measurement made on the item. This allows us to keep information about an item together when the table is sorted or a subset of the rows are selected. Columns can hold different types of information, such as text in one column and numbers in the next. In fact, data tables are one of the most frequently used formats when analyzing data, from spreadsheets to survey results to the tables inside databases. 

In Python, the most popular package for representing and manipulating table data is **pandas**. The pandas package is built around two key data structures: a **Series**, which is a single sequence of values with labels attached, and a **DataFrame** which is a table of data. By the end you will be able to load a file into a table, select the rows and columns you want, add new columns computed from old ones, decide what to do about values that are missing, summarize a table one group at a time, and combine two tables into one. These operations will allow us to answer the questions about flight delays we posed above. 



```{python}

import pandas as pd

```


## From arrays to Series

As mentioned above, the pandas package contains two key data structures: **Series**, and **DataFrames**. Let's start by discussing the pandas Series and once we have understood this data structure we will go on to discuss DataFrames. 

At the end of @sec-array-computations we were storing data on a year of gas prices in two separate NumPy arrays: `gas_prices` held 52 prices as numbers and `gas_dates` held the 52 dates those numbers belonged to. The cell below loads them again, exactly as before.

```{python}

# Try to download the data live from FRED; if that fails (for example, when there
# is no internet connection), fall back to a saved snapshot of the same year.
try:
    from pandas_datareader.fred import FredReader
    gas_data_all = FredReader("GASREGW", start="2024-06-01", end="2026-01-15").read().reset_index()
    gas_year = gas_data_all[(gas_data_all["DATE"] >= "2025-01-01") & (gas_data_all["DATE"] < "2026-01-01")]
except Exception:
    gas_year = pd.read_csv("data/gas_prices_GASREGW_2025.csv", parse_dates=["DATE"])

gas_prices = gas_year["GASREGW"].values
gas_dates = gas_year["DATE"].values

gas_prices[0:3]

```


Because this data was held in separate arrays, nothing in Python knew they belonged together. The connection lived entirely in our own knowledge of the data, and we needed to be very careful to keep these arrays in the same order. Sort the prices to find the cheapest price and the dates no longer line up. Drop a week from one array and every position in the other becomes wrong. It was also difficult to ask the very simple question of given a particular week, what was the price of the gas during that week. 

A **Series** solves this by carrying the labels (called an **Index**) along with the values. The values are just a regular ndarray that we saw in @sec-array-computations and the Index allows us to easily access these array values through a set of labels. 


```{python}
#| echo: false

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import matplotlib.patches as patches

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.4, 3.1))

blue, amber, grey = "#cfe3f7", "#fde2a8", "#7a7a7a"
labels = ["2025-01-06", "2025-01-13", "2025-01-20"]
values = ["3.047", "3.043", "3.109"]

# Left panel: two arrays whose pairing exists only by convention. Right panel:
# one Series in which each label is bound to its value. Both panels are drawn
# from the same row geometry so the two representations line up for comparison.
row_y = [2.0, 1.4, 0.8]
box_w, box_h = 1.05, 0.44

# Everything above the cells is positioned off the cells themselves, so the
# column labels keep their clearance from the dashed bracket if the rows move.
bracket_pad = 0.13
bracket_top = row_y[0] + box_h + bracket_pad + 0.02   # + the boxstyle's own pad
label_y = bracket_top + 0.20
title_y = label_y + 0.52


def cell(x, y, text, colour):
    ax.add_patch(patches.FancyBboxPatch(
        (x, y), box_w, box_h, boxstyle="round,pad=0.012",
        fc=colour, ec="#9ab", lw=1.0))
    ax.text(x + box_w / 2, y + box_h / 2, text, ha="center", va="center", fontsize=8.5)


# --- left: two unconnected arrays ---
for y, lab, val in zip(row_y, labels, values):
    cell(0.15, y, lab, amber)
    cell(1.60, y, val, blue)
ax.text(0.15 + box_w / 2, label_y, "gas_dates", ha="center", fontsize=9,
        family="monospace", color="#7a5a10")
ax.text(1.60 + box_w / 2, label_y, "gas_prices", ha="center", fontsize=9,
        family="monospace", color="#1c4f80")
ax.text(1.45, row_y[1] + box_h / 2, "?", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=15,
        color="#c0392b", style="italic")
ax.text(1.45, 0.30, "Paired only by position", ha="center", fontsize=8.5,
        style="italic", color="#c0392b")

# --- right: one Series ---
x_lab, x_val = 4.05, 5.20
for y, lab, val in zip(row_y, labels, values):
    cell(x_lab, y, lab, amber)
    cell(x_val, y, val, blue)
    # a tie bar showing the two halves are one object
    ax.plot([x_lab + box_w, x_val], [y + box_h / 2] * 2, color=grey, lw=1.4, zorder=0)
ax.text(x_lab + box_w / 2, label_y, "Index", ha="center", fontsize=9,
        family="monospace", color="#7a5a10")
ax.text(x_val + box_w / 2, label_y, "values", ha="center", fontsize=9,
        family="monospace", color="#1c4f80")

# one bracket around the whole Series
ax.add_patch(patches.FancyBboxPatch(
    (x_lab - bracket_pad, row_y[-1] - bracket_pad),
    (x_val + box_w) - x_lab + 2 * bracket_pad,
    (row_y[0] + box_h) - row_y[-1] + 2 * bracket_pad,
    boxstyle="round,pad=0.02", fc="none", ec=grey, lw=1.4, linestyle="--"))
ax.text((x_lab + x_val + box_w) / 2, 0.30, "One object: labels travel with values",
        ha="center", fontsize=8.5, style="italic", color="#2e6b2e")

ax.text(1.68, title_y, "Two NumPy arrays", ha="center", fontsize=10, weight="bold")
ax.text(5.30, title_y, "One pandas Series", ha="center", fontsize=10, weight="bold")

ax.set_xlim(-0.05, 6.6)
ax.set_ylim(0.10, title_y + 0.22)
ax.axis("off")
plt.show()

```


We can create pandas Series by handing pandas the values and the Index labels we want attached to them:

```{python}

# The values come first, then the labels to attach to them
gas = pd.Series(gas_prices, index=gas_dates)

gas.head()

```

When we call the `.head()` method, the left-hand column is the **Index**, which holds the labels, and the right-hand column holds the values. They are now one object, so anything that happens to the values happens to the labels too.

We can extract both the Index values and the data values separately if you want them. Using the `.values` property extracts the same NumPy array we started with, and using the `.index` property returns the Index values:

```{python}

[gas.values[0:3], gas.index[0:3]]

```



### Looking up values by label and by position

We can extract values from a Series object by the position in the Series and by the Index label. To extract data by position, we use `.iloc` which takes a **position**, counting from zero the way a list or an array does, and returns the value at that position.

```{python}

# The first price of the year, by position
gas.iloc[0]

```

To extract a value based on an Index label, we use `.loc` which takes a **label**, (which here means an actual date), and returns the value at that given label.

```{python}

# The price in the week of April 7th, by label
gas.loc["2025-04-07"]

```


It is worth pausing here to make sure you understand the difference between `.iloc` and `.loc` is the single most common source of puzzlement for people new to pandas. The rule to understand them is short:

- `.iloc` is about *where a value sits*; i.e., the position in the array
- `.loc` is about *what it is called*; i.e., the Index name

On this Series above, the label `"2025-04-07"` and the position `13` refer to the same price, but only the former stays correct if the data is sorted or values are removed from the array. 

### All NumPy array operations works for Series

A Series is built on top of a NumPy array, so the vectorized arithmetic and Boolean masking from @sec-array-computations carry over unchanged. Arithmetic applies to every value at once and the Index labels remain unchanged:

```{python}

# Convert every price from dollars to cents
(gas * 100).head(3)

```

A comparison produces a Series of `True` and `False` values, and using it to index the Series keeps the rows where it is `True`:

```{python}

expensive = gas[gas > 3.15]

expensive

```

The difference from a plain NumPy array is visible in that output. The result don't just show us the expensive gas prices but they also show us *which*  weeks were the expensive ones, because each value brought its Index date along with it.

That also means the summary functions can now answer questions in terms of labels. The `.idxmax()` method gives the Index label of the largest value rather than its position which can be much more informative:

```{python}

# Which week of 2025 had the highest average price?
[gas.idxmax(), gas.max()]

```

In @sec-array-computations we could only say that prices peaked sometime in April. With a labeled index we can say that the peak was the week of April 7th, at just over \$3.24, without counting positions by hand.

::: {.callout-tip title="Exercise" #exercise-data_tables-series}

Using the `gas` Series:

1. Find the price in the week of September 1st, 2025.
2. Find the *lowest* price of the year and the week it occurred, using `.idxmin()` and `.min()`.
3. Count how many weeks had a price below \$3.00.

:::

::: {.callout-note title="Solution" #solution-data_tables-series collapse="true"}

```{python}

# 1. A specific week, looked up by its label
gas.loc["2025-09-01"]

```

```{python}

# 2. The cheapest week of the year
[gas.idxmin(), gas.min()]

```

```{python}

# 3. A comparison gives True/False, and summing counts the True values
(gas < 3.00).sum()

```

Prices bottomed out in the last week of December at about \$2.81, and only 5 of the 52 weeks were below \$3.00.

:::


## Tables of data: the DataFrame

A Series holds one column of data. Most data has many columns, and they are rarely all the same kind of data. The dataset we will use for the rest of this chapter records every flight that departed one of New York City's three main airports during 2025 including the date, the airline, where the plane was going, how far it flew, and how late it left. Some of those are numbers, some are text, and a table needs to hold both.

The data comes from the **Bureau of Transportation Statistics**, the U.S. agency that collects on-time performance records from every domestic airline. Run the cell below to load it. As with the loading code in earlier chapters, you do not need to follow the details yet, though by the end of this chapter you will.

```{python}

flights_all_columns = pd.read_csv(
    "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/emeyers/intro_datascience/main/data/nycflights/flights.csv.gz"
)

flights_all_columns.head()

```

Each row is one flight, and the columns contain information about each flight. For example, the `dep_delay` column records how many minutes late it left, and a negative value means it left early.

Like Series objects, DataFrames also have an Index that allows use to refer to rows by labels that are useful. Here the Index are just successive integer values so are not particularly useful. Later in the chapter we will explore setting the Index labels to more meaningful names to do useful operations on particular rows. 

Before computing anything, it is worth finding out how larege the DataFrame is. The `.shape` property gives the number of rows and columns:

```{python}

flights_all_columns.shape

```

As we can see from this output, there are 360,771 flights described by 19 columns. This is the first dataset in this book that would be genuinely painful to handle as lists.

The `.columns` property shows the column names, and `.dtypes` reports what kind of value each column holds:

```{python}

flights_all_columns.dtypes

```

 Notice that `dep_delay` is a floating-point column even though a delay is always a whole number of minutes; that happens because some flights are missing a delay, and the missing marker `NaN` is itself a floating-point value. Also, text here is contained in the `object` data type. 

The `.describe()` method summarizes numeric columns, giving the count, mean, standard deviation and quartiles you met in @sec-descriptive-stats. Let's look at these statistics for just the departure delay column: 

```{python}

# Just the delay column, rounded, so the numbers are readable
flights_all_columns["dep_delay"].describe().round(1)

```

The output shows that the mean departure delay is about 15 minutes, but the median (50% percentile) is **−3** minutes, meaning a typical flight actually pushes back from the gate slightly *early*. The largest delay in the file is 2,590 minutes, which is a little over 43 hours. That gap between mean and median is the signature of a right-skewed distribution, exactly as in @sec-descriptive-stats: most flights are close to on time, and a long tail of severe delays drags the average upward.

A histogram makes the shape visible. Because of that long tail, plotting the raw column would produce a single spike, so we restrict the range to the delays that most flights actually experience:

```{python}

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

plt.hist(flights_all_columns["dep_delay"], edgecolor = "k", bins=40, range=(-30, 120))
plt.xlabel("Departure delay (minutes)")
plt.ylabel("Number of flights")
plt.title("Most flights leave close to on time")
plt.show()

```

The peak sits just below zero, and the tail stretches to the right. Keep this picture in mind, because the rest of the chapter is largely about asking which flights sit in that tail.

::: {.callout-tip title="Exercise" #exercise-data_tables-inspect}

1. How many columns does it have? Get the answer from `.shape` rather than counting.
2. Display the *last* five rows using `.tail()`.
3. Use `.describe()` on the `distance` column. What are the shortest and longest flights in the data?

:::

::: {.callout-note title="Solution" #solution-data_tables-inspect collapse="true"}

```{python}

# 1. .shape gives (rows, columns), so the second value is the column count
flights_all_columns.shape[1]

```

```{python}

# 2. The last five rows
flights_all_columns.tail()

```

```{python}

# 3. Summary of the distance column
flights_all_columns["distance"].describe().round(1)

```

The shortest flight in the data covers 96 miles and the longest 4,983 miles, with half of all flights falling between 544 and 1,391 miles.

:::


## Selecting columns and rows

A table is only useful if you can analyze the parts of it that you are interested in. Pandas separates this into two questions: which columns, and which rows.

### Columns

Passing a single column name in square brackets gives that column back as a Series, the object from the start of this chapter:

```{python}

flights_all_columns["dep_delay"].head()

```

Passing a *list* of names instead gives back a DataFrame containing those columns:

```{python}

flights_all_columns[["carrier", "origin", "dest", "dep_delay"]].head()

```

The difference between those two is a common stumbling block when learning first pandas, because the second form looks like the first with an extra pair of brackets. It helps to read the inner brackets as an ordinary Python list: `flights_all_columns[["carrier", "dest"]]` is asking for *a list of columns*, so the answer is a DataFrame. The `flights_all_columns["carrier"]` is just a single *string* inside the square brackets, so the answer is a Series. Note, a DataFrame is also returned if a list with a single string is also used, so `flights_all_columns[["dest"]]` returns a DataFrame with one column, while `flights_all_columns["dest"]` returns a Series.

Selecting columns is also how we make a table easier to live with. Nineteen columns is more than fits comfortably on a page, and this chapter only needs about half of them, so let us keep those in a table called `flights` and use it from here on:

```{python}

flights = flights_all_columns[["month", "day", "carrier", "flight", "tailnum",
                               "origin", "dest", "dep_delay", "arr_delay",
                               "air_time", "distance", "hour"]].copy()

flights.head()

```

The `.copy()` on the end is the same method used on an array in @sec-array-computations, and it is there for the same reason: it makes `flights` an independent table rather than a view onto the original, so that adding a column to it later cannot disturb `flights_all_columns`.

Every one of the 360,771 flights is still here, since selecting columns does not remove any rows. What has changed is how much of each flight we are carrying: twelve columns instead of nineteen, which is narrow enough to display whole. The original table is still available as `flights_all_columns` whenever one of the columns we dropped is needed.

### Rows

We can extract a subset of rows in the same way they as we did for a Series. In particular, the `.iloc` selects rows by position:

```{python}

# The first three rows
flights.iloc[0:3]

```

We can also select columns based on the Index name using the `.loc` method, in the same way as we did for Series. As mentioned above, the Index names in `flights` DataFrame Iare just successive integers which is not particularly useful. Let's use set the Index to the destination of where the flight is going using the the `.set_index()` method. 

```{python}

flights2 = flights.set_index("dest")

flights2.head()

```

We can then use the the `.loc` method to extract only flights that are going to Miami using: 

```{python}

flights2 = flights2.loc["MIA"] 

flights2.head()

```


We can also return the Index names as as return column using the `reset_index()` method. In this case, it will make `dest` a regular a column again and will once again set the Index to successive integers.

```{python}

flights2 = flights2.reset_index()

flights2.head()

```


Usually, however, the most useful way to extract rows is not by position or by using Index names, but instead "filtering" rows that match particular conditions based on values in particular coloumns. In @sec-array-computations a comparison on a NumPy array produced an array of `True` and `False` values that could be used to keep only the values you wanted. The same idea works on a DataFrame, which is a powerful way to get only rows we are interested in. For example, we can get only the flights that left JFK airport using the code below: 

```{python}

# True for every flight that left from JFK
from_jfk = flights["origin"] == "JFK"

# Extracting just the flights from JFK
flights[from_jfk].head()

```

```{python}

# How many of the year's flights left from JFK?
from_jfk.sum()

```

Conditions can be combined with `&` for "and" and `|` for "or". Each condition needs its own parentheses:

```{python}

# Flights from JFK that left more than an hour late
badly_delayed = flights[(flights["origin"] == "JFK") & (flights["dep_delay"] > 60)]

badly_delayed.shape[0]

```

Nearly nine thousand flights out of JFK left over an hour behind schedule during the year.

::: {.callout-tip title="Exercise" #exercise-data_tables-select}

1. Select just the `carrier`, `flight` and `dest` columns, and show the first three rows.
2. How many flights departed from Newark (`EWR`)?
3. How many flights left from LaGuardia (`LGA`) and flew more than 1,000 miles?

:::

::: {.callout-note title="Solution" #solution-data_tables-select collapse="true"}

```{python}

# 1. A list of column names gives back a table
flights[["carrier", "flight", "dest"]].head(3)

```

```{python}

# 2. A comparison gives True/False, and summing counts the True values
(flights["origin"] == "EWR").sum()

```

```{python}

# 3. Two conditions, each in its own parentheses
long_from_lga = flights[(flights["origin"] == "LGA") & (flights["distance"] > 1000)]

long_from_lga.shape[0]

```

Newark handled 120,286 departures, and 45,087 flights left LaGuardia for a destination more than 1,000 miles away.

:::


## The `.query()` method: A more readible way to filter data

Boolean masking is very common way to get a subset of rows that meet particular conditions, and you will see it everywhere. However the syntax can be a little cumbersome. For example, the name of the table appears three times in a single line in the code below:

```{python}

flights[(flights["origin"] == "JFK") & (flights["dep_delay"] > 60)].shape[0]

```

Pandas also has a `.query()` method, which takes the condition as a string and lets you refer to columns by their names: 

```{python}

flights.query('origin == "JFK" and dep_delay > 60').shape[0]

```

The two give exactly the same 8,889 rows. Inside a query you write `and`, `or` and `not` rather than `&`, `|` and `~`, which is closer to how you would say the condition out loud. Because the whole condition is a string, the quotes have to alternate: the example above wraps the query in single quotes so that the string `"JFK"` inside it can use double ones.

To use a value held in a Python variable, put `@` in front of its name:

```{python}

cutoff = 180

flights.query("dep_delay > @cutoff").shape[0]

```

There is one limitation worth knowing. Because `.query()` refers to columns as though they were variable names, it only works when a column name is a legal Python variable name. A column called `budget_2013$`, like the one in the movie data from @sec-descriptive-stats, cannot be referred to this way since it ends in a dollar sign, so in this case you would need to use Boolean indexing to extract data from this row. Likewise, we can't use the `.query()` method to refer to columns that have spaces in their names. 

Neither style is more correct. Using whichever makes a particular code easier to read is generally perferred.

::: {.callout-tip title="Exercise" #exercise-data_tables-query}

Rewrite each of these using `.query()`, and check that you get the same number of rows:

1. `flights[flights["dest"] == "LAX"]`
2. `flights[(flights["origin"] == "EWR") & (flights["distance"] < 500)]`

:::

::: {.callout-note title="Solution" #solution-data_tables-query collapse="true"}

```{python}

# 1. A single condition on a text column
[flights[flights["dest"] == "LAX"].shape[0],
 flights.query('dest == "LAX"').shape[0]]

```

```{python}

# 2. Two conditions joined with "and" rather than "&"
[flights[(flights["origin"] == "EWR") & (flights["distance"] < 500)].shape[0],
 flights.query('origin == "EWR" and distance < 500').shape[0]]

```

Both pairs agree: 15,496 flights went to Los Angeles, and 21,367 short flights left Newark.

:::


## Adding, renaming, and sorting columns 

A new column can be added to a DataFrame by assigning an array, Series that is the same length as the DataFrame, to a name that does not exist yet.

```{python}

# How much time a flight made up in the air: positive means it caught up
flights["time_made_up"] = flights["dep_delay"] - flights["arr_delay"]

flights[["carrier", "origin", "dest", "dep_delay", "arr_delay", "time_made_up"]].head()

```

Columns are renamed by passing a dictionary, the data structure from @sec-python-basics, whose keys are the old names and whose values are the new ones:

```{python}

flights = flights.rename(columns={"dep_delay": "departure_delay"})

flights.columns

```

That change makes the rest of this chapter harder to read rather than easier, so we will put it straight back:

```{python}

flights = flights.rename(columns={"departure_delay": "dep_delay"})

```


Finally, we can use `.sort_values()` method to reorder the rows by values in a column. By default the values are sorted from smallest to largest. Adding `ascending=False` argument puts the largest first. We can get the flights with the longest delays using: 

```{python}

# The five longest departure delays of the year
flights.sort_values("dep_delay", ascending=False).head(5)

```



::: {.callout-tip title="Exercise" #exercise-data_tables-sort}

1. Create a new DataFrame called `flight_speed` add a column called `speed` holding each flight's average speed in miles per hour, which is `distance` divided by `air_time`, multiplied by 60 because `air_time` is in minutes.
2. Reduce the `flight_speed` DataFrame to only have the columns "origin", "dest", "distance", "air_time", "speed". 
3. Sort the `flight_speed` DataFrame by `speed` to order the data from the fast to the slowest flight and display the 6 flights with the fastest speed.

:::

::: {.callout-note title="Solution" #solution-data_tables-sort collapse="true"}


```{python}

# 1. air_time is in minutes, so multiply by 60 to get miles per hour
flight_speed = flights.copy()

flight_speed["speed"] = (flights["distance"] / flights["air_time"]) * 60

```


```{python}

# 2. Select only the 
flight_speed = flight_speed[["origin", "dest", "distance", "air_time", "tailnum", "speed"]]

```


```{python}

# 3. Sort descending and show the first 6 rows
flight_speed.sort_values("speed", ascending=False).head()

```


The fastest works out at about 837 miles per hour, which ought to give you pause. No airliner cruises that fast, only four flights in the entire year come out above 700, and the median is around 405. The likely explanation is that this flight's recorded air time is wrong, not that the aircraft broke a record. A result that disagrees with what you already know about the world is usually telling you something about a mistake in the data rather than about the world.

:::


## Missing data

When we looked at `.dtypes` earlier, `dep_delay` turned out to be a floating-point column even though a delay is a whole number of minutes, and the reason given was that some flights have no delay recorded at all. Those gaps are not a mistake in the file. A **cancelled flight** still appears in the data, because it was scheduled and then did not happen: it has a scheduled departure time but no actual one, and so no delay. Pandas writes such a missing value as `NaN`.

The `.isna()` method marks every missing value with `True`, and since summing a Boolean column counts the `True` values, the two together count what is missing:

```{python}

flights[["dep_delay", "arr_delay", "tailnum"]].isna().sum()

```

So 8,634 of the year's 360,771 flights never left, about 2.4% of the schedule. That is information rather than an error, and it is worth noticing that the number of missing *arrival* delays is larger still: a flight can take off and then be diverted, so it departs but never arrives where it meant to.

Most calculations skip missing values automatically. The mean delay we computed earlier was the mean of the flights that actually departed, and pandas did that silently. When you want to work only with complete rows, `.dropna()` method removes any rows that contain missing data. Passing `subset=` restricts the check to the columns you care about, which matters here because dropping every row with *any* missing value would also discard the flights whose `tailnum` was never recorded:

```{python}

departed = flights.dropna(subset=["dep_delay"])

[flights.shape[0], departed.shape[0]]

```

Deciding what to do about missing values is a judgment call rather than a technical issue. Dropping the cancelled flights is the right choice when you are asking how late departures run, and the wrong choice when you are asking how reliable an airline is, since cancelling a flight is the most severe way of failing a passenger. The data cannot make that decision for you.

::: {.callout-tip title="Exercise" #exercise-data_tables-missing}

1. How many flights are missing an `air_time`?
2. Cancelled flights have no `dep_delay`. Use a Boolean mask with `.isna()` to select them, and find how many were scheduled to leave JFK.

:::

::: {.callout-note title="Solution" #solution-data_tables-missing collapse="true"}

```{python}

# 1. Count the missing values in one column
flights["air_time"].isna().sum()

```

```{python}

# 2. .isna() gives a True/False column, which selects rows like any other mask
cancelled = flights[flights["dep_delay"].isna()]

(cancelled["origin"] == "JFK").sum()

```

10,284 flights have no recorded air time, and 1,915 of the cancelled flights were due to leave JFK.

:::


## Summarizing by group

Suppose we are interested in calculating the average delay for each airline so that we can avoid the airlines that have the longest average delays.  A convenient format for the results would be a table, where each row corresponds to one airline and there is a column that shows the average delay.  

To create this result table, we need to split the orignal `flights` DataFrame into a separate group for each airline, computing the mean delay within each group, and the collect the results the new result table. That three-step pattern is common enough to have a name, **split-apply-combine**, and `.groupby()` methods performs these steps.

```{python}
#| echo: false

import matplotlib.patches as patches

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.6, 3.3))

blue, amber, green = "#cfe3f7", "#fde2a8", "#d6ecd2"
rows = [("AA", 12), ("B6", 4), ("AA", 20), ("DL", 6), ("B6", 8), ("DL", 10)]
groups = [("AA", [12, 20], 16.0, amber), ("B6", [4, 8], 6.0, blue), ("DL", [6, 10], 8.0, green)]
colour_of = {"AA": amber, "B6": blue, "DL": green}

box_w, box_h = 0.92, 0.34


def cell(x, y, text, colour, width=box_w):
    ax.add_patch(patches.FancyBboxPatch(
        (x, y), width, box_h, boxstyle="round,pad=0.01", fc=colour, ec="#9ab", lw=0.9))
    ax.text(x + width / 2, y + box_h / 2, text, ha="center", va="center", fontsize=8)


# stage 1: the original table, coloured by the group each row belongs to
top = 2.30
for i, (carrier, delay) in enumerate(rows):
    y = top - i * 0.40
    cell(0.10, y, f"{carrier}   {delay}", colour_of[carrier], width=1.30)
ax.text(0.75, top + 0.52, "the table", ha="center", fontsize=9, weight="bold")

# stage 2: split into one block per carrier
x_split = 2.65
y_cursor = top + 0.06
block_centres = []
for carrier, delays, _, colour in groups:
    block_top = y_cursor
    for d in delays:
        cell(x_split, y_cursor, f"{carrier}   {d}", colour, width=1.30)
        y_cursor -= 0.40
    # centre of this block, taken from the rows just drawn rather than guessed
    block_centres.append((block_top + (y_cursor + 0.40)) / 2)
    y_cursor -= 0.18
ax.text(x_split + 0.65, top + 0.52, "split", ha="center", fontsize=9, weight="bold")

# stage 3: one mean per group, positioned at the vertical centre of its block
x_out = 5.55
for (carrier, _, mean, colour), cy in zip(groups, block_centres):
    cell(x_out, cy, f"{carrier}   {mean:.1f}", colour, width=1.30)
ax.text(x_out + 0.65, top + 0.52, "apply, then combine", ha="center", fontsize=9, weight="bold")

# arrows between the stages, labelled at their midpoints
for x0, x1, label in ((1.48, 2.55, "by carrier"), (4.03, 5.45, "mean")):
    ax.annotate("", xy=(x1, 1.30), xytext=(x0, 1.30),
                arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", color="0.35", lw=1.4))
    ax.text((x0 + x1) / 2, 1.40, label, ha="center", fontsize=8.5,
            style="italic", color="0.3")

ax.set_xlim(0.0, 7.2)
ax.set_ylim(-0.05, 3.0)
ax.axis("off")
plt.show()

```

To calculate results separately for each airline, we need to use  `.groupby("carrier")` which forms the groups for each airline. We then use the `.agg()` method to calculate the mean separately for each group. Inside the `.agg()` method we will use the syntax `result_col_name = ("input_col", "agg_function")` where:

- `result_col_name` is the name of the column in the result DataFrame (e.g., `mean_delay`)  
- `"input_col"` is the name of the column we want to apply our aggregate on (e.g., `dep_delay`)
- `"agg_function"` is the name of the function we want to apply (e.g., `mean`)

Using this syntax, we can calcualte the average delay for each airline as:

```{python}

by_carrier = flights.groupby("carrier").agg(
    mean_delay = ("dep_delay", "mean"),
)

by_carrier.round(1)

```

The airline "carrier codes" become the Index in the result DataFrame, which is why they sit to the left in bold. Sorting gives our answer:

```{python}

by_carrier.sort_values("mean_delay", ascending=False).round(1)

```

Looking at the results, we see that F9 (Frontier) is the worst, with a mean delay a little over 27 minutes, and YX (Republic Airline) is the best with a mean delay under 10 minutes.

Before we read too much into the results, however, it is imporant to know how many values when into computing the mean delay for each airline. We can calculate the number of airlines in each group, by creating a second result column called `num_flights` where we use the `count` function as our aggregating function: 

```{python}

flights.groupby("carrier").agg(
    mean_delay = ("dep_delay", "mean"),
    num_flights = ("dep_delay", "count")
).sort_values("mean_delay", ascending=False).round(1)

```

The results show that Frontier's mean delay is calcualted from 6,696 flights, which is plenty, but MQ (Envoy Air) sits second-worst on the strength of only 850 flights, and Hawaiian's 366 flights. If an average is computed from too few data points, then we shouldn't believe the mean results will necessarily be an accurate refleciton of what the true delay might be in the future which is a topic we will discuss more in @sec-statistical-inference. Thus, it is usually important to report the group size alongside the statistic.


::: {.callout-tip title="Exercise" #exercise-data_tables-groupby}

1. Group the flights by `origin` and compute the mean departure delay for each of the three airports.
2. Group by `month` and compute both the mean delay and the number of flights. Which month is worst, and does the answer make sense?

:::

::: {.callout-note title="Solution" #solution-data_tables-groupby collapse="true"}

```{python}

# 1. One row per airport
flights.groupby("origin").agg(mean_delay=("dep_delay", "mean")).round(1)

```

```{python}

# 2. Two statistics per month
by_month = flights.groupby("month").agg(
    flights=("flight", "count"),
    mean_delay=("dep_delay", "mean"),
)

by_month.round(1)

```

The three airports are close together, between about 14 and 16 minutes. The month-by-month pattern is much stronger: July is worst at 28.5 minutes and January best at 8.3. Summer combines the heaviest travel demand with thunderstorm season, and a plane held up by an afternoon storm is late for every leg it flies afterwards.

:::


## Joining two tables

The result above is still hard to read, because `F9` and `YX` are codes rather than names. The codes are explained in a second file, which lists every airline that appears in the data:

```{python}

airlines = pd.read_csv(
    "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/emeyers/intro_datascience/main/data/nycflights/airlines.csv"
)

airlines

```

This is the situation a **join** exists for: two tables that share a column, and hold different information about the same items. The `.merge()` method combines the tables, matching rows wherever the values in a particular column are the same:

```{python}

flights_named = flights.merge(airlines, on="carrier")

flights_named[["carrier", "name", "origin", "dest", "dep_delay"]].head()

```

Looking at the results, we see that every flight has kept its own data and additionally has gained the `name` column from the `airlines` table so now we have a more meaningful name for airline carrier for each flight. 

In the code above, we called the `.merge()` method on the `flights` DataFrame, and we passed the `airlines` DataFrame as an argument to the `.merge()` method. Using the standard terminology for joining tables, we would call the `flights` DataFrame the "left" DataFrame because it appears on the left, and the `airlines` DataFrame the "right" DataFrame because it appears on the right. Additionally, the `on=` argument names the column to match on. When we want to align the DataFrames on by columns with different names, we can use `left_on=` and `right_on=` to specify which columns to use in the left and right DataFrames.

The remaining question is what happens to rows that find no match when we try to line how the values in the columns. That is what `how=` arguments controls, and the four choices are easiest to see drawn:

```{python}
#| echo: false

import numpy as np

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 4, figsize=(7.9, 2.6))

# The two circles, and a pixel grid used to work out which region each point
# falls in. Shading a computed mask rather than the circles themselves is what
# lets each panel highlight exactly the rows a given join keeps.
cx_left, cx_right, cy, radius = 0.40, 0.60, 0.52, 0.27
grid = np.linspace(0, 1, 420)
gx, gy = np.meshgrid(grid, grid)
in_left = (gx - cx_left) ** 2 + (gy - cy) ** 2 <= radius ** 2
in_right = (gx - cx_right) ** 2 + (gy - cy) ** 2 <= radius ** 2

regions = {
    "left_only": in_left & ~in_right,
    "both": in_left & in_right,
    "right_only": in_right & ~in_left,
}
kept_by_join = {
    "inner": ["both"],
    "left": ["left_only", "both"],
    "right": ["both", "right_only"],
    "outer": ["left_only", "both", "right_only"],
}
captions = {
    "inner": "only rows in both",
    "left": "all rows from the left",
    "right": "all rows from the right",
    "outer": "all rows from both",
}

# The outlines are neutral so that colour carries one meaning only: filled means
# the join keeps those rows, pale means they are dropped.
kept_fill = np.array([0.62, 0.79, 0.88])
dropped_fill = np.array([0.94, 0.94, 0.94])
outline = "#1a1a1a"

for ax, (how, kept) in zip(axes, kept_by_join.items()):
    shaded = np.ones(in_left.shape + (3,))
    shaded[in_left | in_right] = dropped_fill
    for region in kept:
        shaded[regions[region]] = kept_fill
    ax.imshow(shaded, origin="lower", extent=(0, 1, 0, 1), interpolation="nearest")

    ax.add_patch(patches.Circle((cx_left, cy), radius, fc="none", ec=outline, lw=1.2))
    ax.add_patch(patches.Circle((cx_right, cy), radius, fc="none", ec=outline, lw=1.2))

    ax.set_title(f'how="{how}"', fontsize=9, family="monospace", pad=6)
    ax.text(0.5, 0.02, captions[how], ha="center", fontsize=7.5,
            style="italic", color="0.3")
    ax.set_xlim(0.02, 0.98)
    ax.set_ylim(-0.02, 1.06)
    ax.axis("off")

# Named once, on the first panel, since the circles mean the same thing in all
# four. The offsets come from the circle geometry so the labels follow it.
axes[0].text(cx_left - radius * 0.62, cy + radius + 0.06, "Left\nDataFrame",
             fontsize=7.5, color=outline, ha="center", va="bottom", linespacing=1.25)
axes[0].text(cx_right + radius * 0.62, cy + radius + 0.06, "Right\nDataFrame",
             fontsize=7.5, color=outline, ha="center", va="bottom", linespacing=1.25)

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

```

The default is `how="inner"`, which keeps only the rows that matched on both DataFrames. Here every carrier in the flights table has an entry in the airlines table, so nothing is lost and the row count is unchanged:

```{python}

[flights.shape[0], flights_named.shape[0]]

```

Checking the size of the DataFrames before and after a join is worth performing every time you join DataFrames. A join that silently drops rows, because a key was spelled differently or one of the DataFrames was incomplete, is one of the easier ways to get a wrong answer that looks entirely reasonable. If you want to be sure nothing is discarded, `how="left"` keeps every row of the left-hand table whether or not it found a match, filling the new columns with `NaN` where it did not. 

We can now put the whole chapter together. Load a table, join it to a second one, group the result, summarize each group, and sort:

```{python}

delay_by_airline = (
    flights
    .merge(airlines, on="carrier")
    .groupby("name")
    .agg(flights=("flight", "count"), mean_delay=("dep_delay", "mean"))
    .sort_values("mean_delay", ascending=False)
)

delay_by_airline.round(1)

```

That is a readable answer to the question we started with, built from five operations that each did one thing.

::: {.callout-tip title="Exercise" #exercise-data_tables-join}

1. Merge `flights` with `airlines`, then find the mean delay for JetBlue flights only.
2. Repeat the airline summary, but group by both `name` and `origin` by passing a list to `.groupby()`. Which airline and airport combination has the worst average delay among pairings with at least 5,000 flights?

:::

::: {.callout-note title="Solution" #solution-data_tables-join collapse="true"}

```{python}

# 1. Merge first, then filter to one airline
jetblue = flights_named[flights_named["name"] == "JetBlue Airways"]

jetblue["dep_delay"].mean().round(1)

```

```{python}

# 2. A list of columns groups by every combination of them
pairs = flights_named.groupby(["name", "origin"]).agg(
    flights=("flight", "count"),
    mean_delay=("dep_delay", "mean"),
)

# Keep only the pairings with enough flights to be meaningful, then sort
big_pairs = pairs[pairs["flights"] >= 5000]

big_pairs.sort_values("mean_delay", ascending=False).round(1).head(5)

```

JetBlue averages 17.6 minutes. Among pairings with at least 5,000 flights, Delta out of Newark is worst at 25.8 minutes, well above Delta's overall figure of 16.3, which suggests the problem lies with that particular operation rather than with the airline as a whole. Note how grouping by two columns produces a row for each combination that actually occurs, rather than for every pairing imaginable.

:::


## Summary

- A **Series** is a one-dimensional column of values with an **index** of labels attached. The labels travel with the values, so filtering or sorting cannot break the correspondence between them.
- `.loc` selects by label and `.iloc` selects by position. Keeping the two apart avoids most early confusion with pandas.
- A **DataFrame** is a table whose columns are Series sharing one index. THe `pd.read_csv()` function reads in a comma-separated-value file and returns a DataFrame.
- One should look at data before computing on it. Using `.head()`, `.shape`, `.dtypes`, `.describe()`, and plotting the data are useful first steps.
- `df["col"]` gives a Series; `df[["col1", "col2"]]` gives a DataFrame.
- Rows are selected with a Boolean mask, the same idea as in @sec-array-computations, or with `.query()` when a string reads more clearly.
- New columns are made by assigning to a new name, and the calculation applies to every row at once.
- A missing value is not always an error. In this data it marks a cancelled flight, and deciding whether to drop such rows depends on the question being asked.
- The `.groupby()` method combined with `.agg()` method performs **split-apply-combine**. One should usually report the size of each group alongside the statistic, because statistics calculated over small groups are unreliable.
- The `.merge()` method joins two tables on a shared column. Check the row count afterwards to be sure the join did not quietly discard data.



## Code summary

The functions and methods introduced in this chapter. Pandas is imported as `pd`.

**Series**

| Code | What it does |
|---|---|
| `pd.Series(values, index=labels)` | Builds a Series, pairing each value with a label |
| `s.index`, `s.values` | The labels, and the values, as separate objects |
| `s.loc[label]` | The value with a given label |
| `s.iloc[position]` | The value at a given position, counting from zero |
| `s.idxmax()`, `s.idxmin()` | The *label* of the largest or smallest value |

**Loading a table and looking at it**

| Code | What it does |
|---|---|
| `pd.read_csv(path)` | Reads a CSV file, from a filename or a URL, into a DataFrame |
| `df.head()`, `df.tail()` | The first or last few rows |
| `df.shape` | The number of rows and columns |
| `df.columns`, `df.dtypes` | The column names, and the kind of value each column holds |
| `df.describe()` | Count, mean, standard deviation and quartiles for each numeric column |

**Selecting columns and rows**

| Code | What it does |
|---|---|
| `df["col"]` | One column, as a Series |
| `df[["a", "b"]]` | Several columns, as a DataFrame |
| `df.loc[label]` | Rows by index label, once a meaningful index has been set |
| `df.iloc[0:3]` | Rows by position |
| `df[df["col"] > 5]` | Keeps the rows where a condition is `True` |
| `df.query('col > 5')` | The same idea written as a string, using `and` and `or` |
| `df.copy()` | An independent copy, needed before adding a column to a selection |

**Changing a table**

| Code | What it does |
|---|---|
| `df["new"] = ...` | Adds a column, computed for every row at once |
| `df.sort_values("col")` | Reorders the rows; `ascending=False` puts the largest first |
| `df.rename(columns={"old": "new"})` | Renames columns, using a dictionary of old to new |
| `df.set_index("col")`, `df.reset_index()` | Makes a column the index, or turns the index back into a column |

**Missing values**

| Code | What it does |
|---|---|
| `df.isna()` | Marks every missing value with `True` |
| `df.isna().sum()` | Counts the missing values in each column |
| `df.dropna(subset=["col"])` | Removes the rows that are missing a value in the named columns |

**Grouping and combining**

| Code | What it does |
|---|---|
| `df.groupby("col")` | Splits the rows into groups sharing a value |
| `.agg(name=("col", "mean"))` | Computes one statistic per group, naming the result |
| `df.merge(other, on="key")` | Joins two tables on a shared column |
| `how="inner"`, `"left"`, `"right"`, `"outer"` | Controls which unmatched rows a merge keeps |

::: {.callout-tip title="Exercise" #exercise-data_tables-babynames}

Load the baby-name data from @sec-introduction and answer the question that chapter left hanging: in what year was a given name most popular?

```{python}
#| eval: false

names = pd.read_csv(
    "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/emeyers/intro_datascience/main/data/babynames/baby_names_all.csv.gz"
)

```

Pick a name, select the rows for that name and one sex, and use `.idxmax()` with `.loc` to find the year in which its `percent` was highest.

:::

::: {.callout-note title="Solution" #solution-data_tables-babynames collapse="true"}

```{python}

names = pd.read_csv(
    "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/emeyers/intro_datascience/main/data/babynames/baby_names_all.csv.gz"
)

# Two conditions: the name we want, and one sex
mary = names[(names["name"] == "Mary") & (names["sex"] == "girl")]

peak = mary.loc[mary["percent"].idxmax()]

peak[["year", "name", "count", "percent"]]

```

Mary peaked in 1880, the first year in the data, when 7.24% of girls were given the name. This is the code @sec-introduction showed you and asked you to take on trust.

:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Exercise" #exercise-data_tables-bechdel}

Load the Bechdel test movie data from @sec-descriptive-stats, which you previously handled as lists:

```{python}
#| eval: false

movies = pd.read_csv("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/fivethirtyeight/data/refs/heads/master/bechdel/movies.csv")

```

Group the movies by `binary`, which records whether each one passed or failed, and compute the number of films and the median `budget_2013$` in each group. What do you find?

:::

::: {.callout-note title="Solution" #solution-data_tables-bechdel collapse="true"}

```{python}

movies = pd.read_csv("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/fivethirtyeight/data/refs/heads/master/bechdel/movies.csv")

movies.groupby("binary").agg(
    films=("title", "count"),
    median_budget=("budget_2013$", "median"),
)

```

Films that pass the test were made on noticeably smaller budgets: a median of about \$31.7 million against \$44.9 million for those that fail. This was the finding behind FiveThirtyEight's original article. Notice what it does *not* establish: the data records what budgets were assigned, not why, and the question of whether studios were funding these films less generously is one the table alone cannot settle.

:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Exercise" #exercise-data_tables-dest}

Which destinations do flights leave New York for most often? Group the flights by `dest`, count them, and show the ten most common. Then find the mean delay for flights to those destinations.

:::

::: {.callout-note title="Solution" #solution-data_tables-dest collapse="true"}

```{python}

by_dest = flights.groupby("dest").agg(
    flights=("flight", "count"),
    mean_delay=("dep_delay", "mean"),
)

by_dest.sort_values("flights", ascending=False).head(10).round(1)

```

Chicago O'Hare and Atlanta come first, both of them major connecting hubs, followed by Orlando. The mean delays across these ten busy routes sit within about five minutes of one another, between 14.5 and 19.6, so no single destination stands out as unusually troubled.

:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Exercise" #exercise-data_tables-weekend}

The `hour` column records the hour a flight was scheduled to leave. Flights scheduled later in the day tend to run later, because a delay early in the day is carried by the same aircraft all afternoon.

Group the flights by the `hour` column and compute the mean departure delay for each hour. Then plot the result with `plt.plot()` to see the pattern.

:::

::: {.callout-note title="Solution" #solution-data_tables-weekend collapse="true"}

```{python}

by_hour = flights.groupby("hour").agg(mean_delay=("dep_delay", "mean"))

plt.plot(by_hour.index, by_hour["mean_delay"], ".-")
plt.xlabel("Scheduled departure hour")
plt.ylabel("Mean departure delay (minutes)")
plt.title("Delays accumulate through the day")
plt.show()

```

Delay climbs steadily from under 3 minutes in the early morning to over 30 by 10pm. The first flights of the day leave close to on time because their aircraft spent the night at the gate; every later flight inherits whatever delay the day has accumulated so far. The dip in the final hour should be treated with care rather than read as good news: only 87 flights all year were scheduled to leave at 11pm, against more than 19,000 at 8pm, so that last point is an average over a very small group.

:::
